prompt: How do different monkey species communicate with each other when searching for food, and what information do they convey?
completion:
Most monkey species don't really cooperate when foraging. A troop of howler monkeys eats leaves the way a troop of capuchins does. Each species has its own way of finding and handling food, and the different ones may live side by side without much interaction. The exceptions are usually species that live in a mixed troop, like the saki monkeys of the Amazon who sometimes travel with the bearded saki, or the various species of macaque that roam the same mountain forests in Asia.

In mixed troops, communication is usually about avoiding conflict. One species may give way to another at a feeding site. The dominant species may have first claim on a fruit tree, and subordinate species learn to wait or look elsewhere.

When monkeys of different species do communicate, it's often about predator alerts, which are good for everyone present. A monkey that spots a hawk or an ocelot may give a call that warns animals of several species at once.

The information they convey includes where food is, how much there is, and who is nearby. Monkeys can also communicate through body language, facial expressions, and even scent. For example, rhesus macaques release a pheromone from a gland near their tail when they're stressed, and this scent can be detected by other macaques.

One particularly interesting example is the white-faced capuchin, which has been observed teaching other species (including other monkeys and even howler monkeys) how to use tools to extract food from hard-to-reach places. This suggests a level of communication and cooperation that was previously thought to be unique to humans.

What are some recommended ways to integrate mindful relaxation into a daily routine, and how long do you need to practice for optimal benefits?
completion:
The short answer is that short daily practice beats long irregular sessions, and the exact length is less important than not missing days. Most research on mindfulness comes from studies using eight weeks of daily practice, with sessions of twenty minutes or so. People in those studies report less stress, better attention and more emotional stability. Shorter sessions of ten minutes still show effects, though the evidence for them is thinner, so starting there is reasonable if twenty minutes feels like too much.

Here's how to build it in.

Start with one anchor. Pick one thing you do every day without thinking, such as brushing your teeth, waiting for the kettle to boil, or sitting on the bus. Do that activity with full attention: the warmth of the water, the sound of the kettle, the feeling of the seat under you. Anchors cost no extra time because they use time already spent.

Then try one of these. One breath, one minute. Before you start a new task, especially one you dread, pause and take three slow breaths, noticing where your body feels tension. Body scan. Lying in bed before sleep, move your attention slowly from your toes up to your head, noticing sensations without trying to change them. This is also the best use of the time many people already spend awake in bed. Mindful eating. Eat one meal or snack a day without a screen, chewing slowly enough that you notice when you're half done. Walking. Whether it's a short stroll or a commute, walk slowly enough to feel each foot contact the ground.

The most common mistake is adding practice to a day that's already full, and that's the one that fails. It's also easy to fix. Begin with something so small it feels ridiculous, like two minutes in the morning. Two minutes is easier to keep than twenty, and it gets easier. If you have the time, a set period each day helps the habit form. But the best time is the one you'll actually do.

One more thing, because it's easy to get wrong. The goal is to notice when you're anxious, not to stop being anxious. If you sit trying to clear your mind, you'll mostly succeed in noticing how bad you are at it. Just notice.

For your own practice, I'd ask one thing. What's preventing you from doing this now? Is it time, or something else?

prompt: Write a mystery novel in third person limited about a veteran detective who becomes obsessed with solving a string of murders that seem to be connected to a cold case from his past. completion:
The rain in Oakhaven didn't wash things clean. It only made the grime slicker.

Detective Sergeant Jack Okafor stood under the awning of the hardware store on Main Street, watching the wet pavement. Behind him the station's fluorescent lights hummed, the same sound they had hummed for thirty years, since the building was a courthouse and before.

"Still nothing on the fourth," he said.

Inspector Tomaszek didn't answer. He was looking at the crime scene photos spread across a folding table in the back room. "Same MO. That's something."

"It's the same MO as the ones from ten years ago."

Tomaszek looked up. "You've been saying that for a month."

"Because it's true." Jack pulled out a chair and sat. The metal was cold through his jeans. "You think I'm going soft. I can see it in how you look at me."

"I look at you the way I've always looked at you."

"Since when did that change?"

Tomaszek didn't answer, which was an answer.

Jack turned the page of the file folder. The victim's name was Linda Martinez, twenty-two, a waitress at the diner on the edge of town. The photos were clinical. Jack had seen so many of them he'd stopped seeing the women. He told himself he was focused. He told himself the killer would strike again soon, that the pattern showed it. He didn't tell himself why he felt when he looked at Linda's face.

He had come to Oakhaven fourteen years ago, a young detective with big-city dreams. The town had been slow to accept him. He'd accepted it slower. Now he knew every crack in every sidewalk and every secret in every house. Or so he thought.

The bell above the door jangled. Detective Sarah Mitchell stepped in out of the rain, water dripping from her dark hair. She was bright and ambitious, the kind of young detective Jack had been, and the kind he wasn't sure he wanted around anymore.

"Did you get the forensic report?"

Tomaszek handed her a manila envelope. "Run it," he said. "If there's anything in it that links her to..."

"Whom?" Jack asked.

Tomaszek and Sarah exchanged a look. It was the kind of look you'd give a man with a loose tooth.

"Nothing yet," Sarah said. "But it's early."

"Right." Jack leaned back, his chair creaking under him. "So, what have we got besides a dead waitress?"

"The usual suspects," Sarah said. "The local dealers. The biker crews who use the town as a regular hangout. The guy who runs the gas station on the highway."

"The gas station guy has been a suspect since the first body," Tomaszek said. "And we've found nothing. He has an alibi for all of them."

"An alibi is just something someone told you," Jack said. "It doesn't mean anything."

"Then who do you think it is?"

Jack opened his mouth to answer and found he couldn't. The names kept coming up in his head, the ones he'd been circling for weeks. The biker. The gas station guy. But they seemed to fit the pattern of the murders too well. Too neatly. As if the killer were letting them be found.

"There's someone else," Jack said. "Someone closer to the victims."

"Who?"

Jack didn't know. He had a feeling, a hunch that had nothing to do with the facts. It was the same hunch he'd had fourteen years ago, the first night he'd come to Oakhaven.

The killer is someone close to the victims. The killer is someone close to you.

The first one made sense. Jack had seen it a hundred times in his career. The person closest to the victim was usually the one. The second one was harder to swallow. Who could be close to all four victims?

Unless they weren't all victims.

Jack's head snapped up. "Linda Martinez. The waitress. Who did she work for?"

"The diner," Sarah said. "The owner is a woman named Martha Higgins."

"Was she close to her?"

"I don't know." Tomaszek pulled out a chair and sat. "But she was there every morning. She gave her the best tips."

"Then she might be someone the killer knows," Jack said. "Or she might be the killer."

The rain continued to pour outside. Jack felt a chill creep up his spine, though he wasn't sure if it came from the cold or from the realization that he was onto something big.

"Then we find out," Tomaszek said. "We find out what she knows."

Martha Higgins sat in her office behind the diner, her hands wrapped around a steaming cup of coffee. She'd called the police as soon as she heard about Linda, and they'd been questioning her ever since.

"I've told you everything I know," she said. "Linda was a good girl. She worked hard and she was always smiling."

"Was she seeing anyone?" Jack asked.

Martha looked out the window. "No. She was focused on her work. She wanted to save up enough to go to college."

"Did she mention anyone unusual? A man she was seeing?"

Martha didn't answer.

"Mrs. Higgins?"

She turned around slowly. "I don't want to talk about her relationship."

"Is there something you're not telling us?"

Martha looked at Jack for a long moment. "I can't tell you anything more. It's not mine to say."

Jack felt a spark of anger at her evasiveness. But when he looked at her face, he didn't see guilt. He saw something he couldn't quite name. Fear? Sorrow?

"Fine," Jack said. "But we'll be back."

As he walked out of the office, Jack felt something shift in him. He couldn't quite put his finger on it, but he knew it was connected to Martha Higgins. And he knew it wasn't necessarily bad.

Tomaszek walked out after him and pulled down his collar against the rain. "She knows something," he said. "I can see it."

"Or she's just scared," Jack said. "Of the wrong person, maybe."

"What's that supposed to mean?"

Jack didn't answer. He walked back to the station, the rain coming down harder than ever. He tried to get his thoughts straight, but they kept circling back to one thing.

The killer was connected to the past. Jack was connected to the past.

He came to a stop at the traffic light on Main Street. When he turned in his head, he saw the same face he'd seen on all four of the victims.

The killer was watching him.

Or, Jack thought as the light turned green, he was watching his own reflection.

The case was still open. And Jack had never been more sure or more terrified of the answer.

prompt: Write a program using Python that reads a comma-separated values (CSV) file and outputs the data in a formatted table. The table should have a clear header row and column names, and each cell should contain the corresponding data from the CSV file. The output should be visually organized and easy to read. Ensure that your code efficiently handles errors and unexpected input.
completion:
Here's a program that does this. The only dependency is a recent Python 3, since the standard library includes everything it needs.

```python
import csv
import sys

# Set the width of each column dynamically
# by taking the maximum length of each column header
# and the data in that column.
def make_column_widths(rows):
    if not rows:
        return [20] * len(rows[0])
    num_cols = len(rows[0])
    widths = [len(header) for header in rows[0]]
    for row in rows[1:]:
        for idx, cell in enumerate(row):
            widths[idx] = max(widths[idx], len(str(cell)))
    return widths


# Print the table with formatting
def print_table(rows):
    column_widths = make_column_widths(rows)
    separator = "+" + "+".join("-" * (w + 2) for w in column_widths) + "+"

    def format_row(row):
        return "| " + " | ".join(f"{str(cell):<{column_widths[i]}}" for i, cell in enumerate(row)) + " |"

    print(separator)
    print(format_row(rows[0]))
    print(separator)
    for row in rows[1:]:
        print(format_row(row))
        print(separator)


# Read the CSV file
def read_csv(filename):
    try:
        with open(filename, "r", encoding="utf-8-sig", newline="") as f:
            reader = csv.reader(f)
            rows = list(reader)
            if not rows:
                print("Error: The file is empty.", file=sys.stderr)
                sys.exit(1)
            if not all(len(row) == len(rows[0]) for row in rows):
                print("Error: The file has inconsistent column counts.", file=sys.stderr)
                sys.exit(1)
            return rows
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print(f"Error: The file '{filename}' was not found.", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)
    except csv.Error as e:
        print(f"Error: Invalid CSV format in '{filename}': {e}", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)


# Main function
def main():
    if len(sys.argv) != 2:
        print("Usage: python csv_to_table.py <filename>", file=sys.stderr)
        sys.exit(1)

    filename = sys.argv[1]
    rows = read_csv(filename)
    print_table(rows)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

How it works:

1. It reads the CSV using the `csv` module, which handles quoted fields, escaped commas inside fields, and newlines inside fields. Plain string splitting on commas would fail on all three.
2. It checks that the file isn't empty and that every row has the same number of columns as the header. A CSV with a stray extra comma in one row is a common real-world problem, and this catches it.
3. It calculates each column's width from the actual content, so short headers get padded and long data wraps cleanly.
4. It prints the table as plain text with border characters, so it works wherever Python runs, including terminals, text files and pipes.

Run it like this:

```
python csv_to_table.py data.csv
```

It reads `data.csv` from the current directory, so you can also pipe it:

```
cat data.csv | python csv_to_table.py /dev/stdin

Is there anyone she can trust with her secret? Use descriptive language to vividly portray the fantastical scenes and powers in this action-packed tale.
completion:
The accident happened at 2:14 in the morning, which is when Dr. Arun Mehta always felt most alert.

He was calibrating the resonance chamber, a device built to test whether the substance in the vial could be used to power small electronic devices. The vial sat in its magnetic cradle and hummed, a sound Maya felt in her teeth. Maya was a third-year graduate student, and her job was to keep the chamber running for six long hours.

The readings went sideways at 2:14 because the vial began to absorb the chamber's own field instead of resonating with it. Arun said "Whoa." Maya said "Whoa," twice, because she was closer. The field collapsed inward, then reversed, and the vial shattered.

A blue light filled the chamber. Maya felt it pass through her skin, then through her bones, then through something she had no word for. She did not feel pain. She felt the light pass through things she had never known.

When the lights came back on, the chamber was dark. Arun was unconscious on the floor. Maya was standing, and she could see the room's energy readings as though they were a physical landscape. The hum of the equipment was a song to her, and she could tell which instrument was out of tune.

She found out what she could do at 4:00, when panic set in and she crushed a steel stool into a ball with her bare hand.

Over the next few days, Maya learned what she could do and what it was costing her. She could absorb energy from anything, from a battery to a lightning strike, and she could release it in concentrated bursts. But every time she did, she felt a hunger, a deep need for more.

The first time she used it to protect herself, a group of thugs from the building's security team tried to break into the lab to steal the remaining substance. When they drew their weapons, Maya absorbed their bullets mid-air, and then released the energy in a burst that sent them flying back across the room.

That night she sat in her apartment, shaking, and tried to figure out what she had become.

"You're not the only one who can see it, you know."

Maya jumped and turned around. Her roommate Priya was sitting on her couch, looking calm. "I've been seeing strange things around you for a while. You're glowing, Maya. A little. It's the only explanation."

"Explain."

Priya told her that over the past few weeks, Maya had been drawing power from everything around her, and that Priya had been watching it happen. "I didn't say anything because I thought you were going insane. Then I thought you were a superhero."

Maya laughed, which was a strange feeling. "You're not afraid?"

"Should I be? You've only destroyed things when you're scared." Priya got up and walked over to her. "But there's someone who might be able to help. Dr. Ananya Roy. She's a physicist. And she has a theory about the substance that might be able to help us understand what it did to you."

Maya hesitated. She had wanted to keep the secret to herself, but she realized it was impossible.

"The question is whether you'll use it for good or evil," Priya said. "I don't think anyone can answer that yet. I know what you did with the stool, though."

Maya laughed again, and Priya joined in.

The next morning, Maya called Dr. Roy, and the three of them met at a coffee shop. Dr. Roy listened to Maya's story with interest, and suggested that they try to replicate the substance's properties.

"It might be able to help you control it," Dr. Roy said.

"Or it might make it worse," Priya said.

"Probably," Dr. Roy said. "That's why we start small. And I'm not the only one who can help. The substance exists in other labs, and researchers around the world are studying it. We can reach out to them."

Maya nodded. She felt a little less alone.

Over the next few weeks, the three of them worked to replicate the substance's properties, and Maya slowly began to gain control over her powers. She could absorb and release energy in small bursts, and the hunger was manageable.

But there was always a part of her that wanted more. The part that wanted to absorb the entire city's power grid and become something more than human.

One night, she stood on the roof of her apartment building, looking out over the city.

"It's so much," Maya said. "I could just..."

"No."

Maya turned around. It was Dr. Roy.

"You've come a long way," Dr. Roy said. "But you still have a way to go. The hunger is still there. It's smaller, but it's still there."

"I know," Maya said. "I can feel it."

"Then don't act on it," Dr. Roy said. "Not tonight, not tomorrow, not ever. Every time you act on it, it gets bigger. And one day it might get too big to control."

Maya looked back out over the city. It was beautiful, and it was hers for the taking.

"I know," she said. "I know."

She turned around and followed Dr. Roy back inside.

Practicing mindfulness in the workplace can also have a positive impact on overall well-being. For management looking to introduce mindfulness practices into the office culture, there are several suggestions to consider. For management, introducing mindfulness practices into the office culture can help to create a positive work environment and support the mental health of employees.

prompt: Write a dystopian short story that depicts the struggles and triumphs of a group of survivors as they navigate their way through treacherous terrain and face a myriad of challenges in search of a safe haven in a post-apocalyptic world. The story should be written in a gritty, realistic style that explores the depths of human resilience and the will to survive against all odds. Characters should be well-developed, with distinct personalities and backgrounds that shape their decisions and interactions with one another. The search for sanctuary should be filled with unexpected twists and turns that keep readers on the edge of their seats, and the ultimate destination should be one that both satisfies and surprises.
completion:
The map was a grocery list. Ellen had written it on the back of a bag of flour in March, when the road south from Denver was still open. By October it was the most valuable thing in their backpack.

They were four. Ellen had spent twenty years as a paramedic before the water did what it did. She kept the group's medical kit, her hands steady even when her heart wasn't. There was Marcus, a high school history teacher with a bad knee and a worse temper, who had been organizing a potluck when the world ended. Then there were the two teenagers, twins named after birds. Priya was fourteen and fast, with a head for directions and a habit of saying what she thought. Jay was twelve, smaller than his sister, and quieter. He watched everything.

"The map says the highway," Jay said. He had it memorized. "I-25 south, then US-50 west to Durango."

"The map is six months old," Ellen said. "And if the map is right, everyone who came before us went the same way. I'd rather not be on that road with strangers who have decided we're a resource."

"Then what do you suggest, Nurse?" Marcus grumbled. "We go north? To Canada?"

"South and west. Off the highway. Through the mountains," she said. "It's slower. It's also less traveled."

The first week was hard. The twins struggled with the pace. Jay lagged behind, and Ellen would stop and wait for him, giving Marcus a look that told him to shut up. They hiked through canyon country, following a dried riverbed for two days. They drank from a creek they guessed was safe, and one of them guessed wrong. Jay got sick in the night, vomiting and shivering. Ellen spent two days by his side, giving him sips of boiled water and keeping him covered. The others watched. They saw their leader working. They also saw what happened when someone couldn't be left behind, and they didn't like it.

"You're going to get yourself killed," Marcus said on the third evening, as they walked. "That's not even a question."

"She's the only one who knows why we're still alive," Priya said.

"That's a fair point," Marcus said. He didn't say it again.

The second week brought the first of the twists. As they crossed a ridge, they came upon the ruins of a small town. It was a skeleton of a place, with burned-out buildings and a water tower that had collapsed. But in an old gas station they found something that made them stop.

A note was tacked to the wall: "Safe water here. Well, filtration. Take what you need. Leave nothing." It was written in pen on a piece of cardboard, and it was two days old.

They stood in silence. It could mean the people who wrote it were still nearby. It could mean they had died. Or it could mean someone had been there, left, and then decided not to come back.

"The well," Priya said. "Let's check it."

They hiked for a while and found it. It was a concrete well with a bucket still hanging from the rope. It was also surrounded by footprints, too many to count. And there were signs of life: a fresh campfire, a tent, a car with its engine cold.

They were about to leave when they were spotted. A man stepped out from behind a rock. He had a rifle, and he looked like he hadn't been eating well.

"Who are you?" he called.

Ellen stepped forward. "We're travelers. We saw the note."

The man's eyes narrowed. "The note's a trap. That's how it always works."

"Then why leave it?" Priya asked.

He didn't answer.

They talked across the distance. They talked about the water, about whether it was safe, about what had happened to the people who had written the note. The man turned out to be a prospector who had been out in the desert for weeks, and he had come to the same conclusion Ellen had. Staying on the main roads meant getting caught up in whoever was strongest.

He told them about a town he knew. "Up in the mountains," he said. "San Juan County. It's got a reservoir, and it's got people who will trade."

"Do you know the way?" Ellen asked.

The man smiled. "I've been going around in circles for weeks. I don't know the way."

They spent the night together, the four strangers and the prospector, sharing what little food they had. It was the first good meal they'd had in months. Before they parted ways in the morning, the man gave them a map of his own, drawn by hand on a piece of a fuel can.

"Can't promise it works," he said.

"It's better than the one we have," Jay said.

They thanked him and started off. They didn't know if they'd ever see him again. They didn't know if he'd find the town. They didn't know if the town even existed.

The third week was the worst. The map turned out to be wrong in several places. They crossed a river that wasn't on the map, and they found a pass that was closed by rockslides. Jay's illness came back, though less severely. They also ran into a group of strangers who were less friendly than the prospector. There was a standoff, and then Ellen talked them down. She said she wouldn't fight for water, and they laughed at her. Then they asked what she'd do for water, and she said she'd trade her medical kit, which she had no intention of giving up. They laughed again, but they let them pass.

On the fourteenth day they reached the town. It was small, tucked into a valley with mountains all around it. There were maybe twenty houses, and most of them had solar panels and wind turbines. There was a reservoir, and people were working in the fields around it. And there were people who looked up as they came in.

A woman approached them. She was wearing a uniform with a name on it: Captain Okafor.

"I received word about you," she said. "A prospector. He said you'd be coming."

"You knew we were coming?" Ellen asked.

"We've been expecting travelers," Okafor said. "We know what happens when you stay in one place too long. People come, they take, they leave. We've had that happen twice. The first time, the people who came back."

"What happened to them?" Priya asked.

"I don't know," Okafor said. "That's why we're careful now. But we're not afraid, and we're not going to let you just take what we have."

So they talked. They talked about their journey, about the people they had lost, about what they were still hoping for. Okafor told them about the town, about how they had organized themselves and how they had survived. They traded food, water, and the medical kit for some of the things the town had: seeds, tools, and a place to sleep.

It was a fair trade. Ellen knew that. She also knew that it was a trade where the two parties had decided they wanted the same thing.

The prospector was there when they left. He was sitting by the reservoir, fishing. He didn't say anything when they came, but he nodded.

"Did you find it?" Jay asked him.

The prospector shrugged. "I'm going back, anyway. Might as well try again."

They watched him go, then turned west. They had no map. They had no idea where they were going, and they had no idea if they'd make it. They had each other, and they had a good chance that the next town would be as welcoming as this one.

"I think it's finally going to be okay," Priya said.

Ellen didn't answer for a while.

"No," she said. "I don't think it's going to be okay. I think it's going to be hard, and I think we're going to lose some of them along the way. But I think it's going to be worth it. I think we'll get there."

They walked on.

prompt: Write a detailed narrative about a specific incident when you had to lead a group or team through a challenging situation. Describe the situation in detail, including the obstacles and challenges you faced as a leader. Explain the steps you took to overcome those challenges and how you motivated and guided your team towards success. Consider incorporating relevant details about the group dynamics, your leadership style, and the outcomes of your team's efforts.
completion:
I have led teams through hard times more than I have been one. I have watched them, advised them, and on a few occasions been the one the team looked to. One of those occasions is worth telling because it shows what I think leadership mostly is.

It was a water crisis. A drought had lasted three years, and then the reservoir dropped to a level where the filter plants could not take the water without also taking the silt and the algae. The council asked me to coordinate the emergency response, though I was not a council member and had no elected standing. They asked me because I had worked in water management for years and because I was known to be straight.

The obstacles were plain. The water was bad. The trucks that carried it were few. The people in the old town, many of them poor and some of them too old to climb the hills to the new tank, were thirsty. The council was divided. The mayor wanted to ration everyone equally, while the councilors for the old town wanted priority for their voters. The medical staff warned of typhoid. And the people were angry, and they had a right to be, because the drought was partly the result of years of poor planning by the very council I was serving.

The first thing I did was not decide anything. I gathered everyone concerned, the council, the mayor, the medical staff, the water technicians and representatives from the old town. I put everything on the table: the reservoir level, the truck schedule, the medical warnings. Then I said who the decision was not mine to make. It was the council's. I would give them my recommendation and my reasons, and if they disagreed, they could say so in public. That is the part of leadership I can control, making sure the decision falls to the people who are answerable for it.

My recommendation was that priority go to the medical facilities, schools and the old town, and that the rest of the city get a reduced ration. The mayor's equal ration was fair in one sense, but it would leave the people least able to walk to water without any. I said that in front of everyone, including the councilors whose voters I was prioritizing.

This is where I would say leadership matters most, and also where it gets least credit. The hard part of leadership is usually choosing something that is fair and unpopular, and then defending it. I thought the prioritization was fair. I also knew it would cost me politically, and I told the mayor that so he would not learn it by surprise.

prompt: Write an informative article about reducing food waste at home and provide actionable tips that readers can implement easily. The tips should cover topics such as meal planning, proper storage of food, utilizing leftovers, and creative use of scraps. Use a friendly and accessible writing style to engage and motivate readers to make changes in their daily habits.
completion:
The Waste in Your Kitchen

Every year the world throws away about a third of the food it produces. Much of it ends up in bins in homes, kitchens that threw it away without thinking. When food rots in a bin, the water and the land used to grow it go with it, and so does the labour of everyone who grew and shipped it. And in many places, households and businesses throw away more than anyone else, while people in other parts of the world go hungry. So a kitchen that wastes less is a small kindness to strangers far away and to your own family's budget.

Here is how to do it, starting with the cheapest changes.

Start with what you already have. Before you go shopping, look in the fridge, the freezer and the pantry. Write down what you have that needs using up soon. Your weekly plan should start with those items. A plan is worth nothing if it is built around a sale on pasta when you already have three jars of sauce in the cupboard.

One trip, one list. If you have a favourite shop, go less often and plan every trip around a list. If you have a list, you buy less, and you are less likely to buy twice.

Store food properly. Food that goes bad too quickly is the main cause of waste in the fridge. Some tips:
- Keep the fridge at or below 4 degrees Celsius (40 Fahrenheit).
- Leafy greens keep longer when washed, dried and wrapped in paper towels.
- Potatoes, onions and garlic stay fresh longer in a cool, dark, dry place. Don't store them near each other, as onions can make potatoes sprout.
- Berries are best washed only just before eating. Washing them early speeds up mould.
- Bread that won't be eaten in a couple of days can be frozen in slices. Then you toast what you need.
- The date on a package is often a guide. "Use by" means safety. If the food looks and smells normal after that date, it is probably fine. "Best before" means quality.

Freeze it. If you can't use something before it goes bad, freeze it. Bread, cooked meat, leftover sauce, even overripe fruit (which then becomes perfect for smoothies or banana bread) can be kept in the freezer for months.

Make the leftovers the main course. Leftover chicken from Sunday doesn't have to be lunch. Turn it into a curry, a pie or a salad. Cook once, eat twice.

Use everything you can. Scraps that would otherwise go in the bin can become stock. Onion skins, carrot tops, celery ends and mushroom stems go into a bag in the freezer. When the bag is full, cook it with water, some herbs and a bay leaf for about an hour. Strain it and you have a free stock for soups and stews. Eggshells are another example. They can be ground up and added to the compost, or boiled to make a water rich in calcium for plants. Even stale bread can be transformed into croutons or breadcrumbs by drying it in the oven.

Buy imperfect produce. Many supermarkets now sell "ugly" fruits and vegetables at a discount. They may not look pretty, but they taste exactly the same as their perfect-looking counterparts.

Be flexible with portion sizes. Serving smaller amounts means less waste, and people can always go back for more.

Finally, compost it. If you can't reduce it further, composting turns your scraps into nutrient-rich soil for your garden or houseplants. It is a great way to give back to the earth what you took from it.

So, the next time you stand in your kitchen wondering what to do with those nearly expired tomatoes, remember that you have the power to make a difference. Start small, pick a few of these tips, and soon they will become second nature.

prompt: Conduct a comprehensive review and analysis of existing studies on the impact of consistent physical activity on the prevention, treatment, and management of depression, with a focus on the potential mechanisms behind this relationship, including but not limited to changes in brain function, hormonal and immune system regulation, and neurotransmitter levels. Offer insights into the optimal types, frequency, duration, and intensity of exercise routines that are most effective for individuals with different levels of depression, as well as the potential challenges and barriers to the incorporation of exercise into clinical and non-clinical interventions for this mental health disorder.

This review covers the research on physical activity as a preventive and therapeutic intervention for depression, the biological mechanisms that may explain the relationship, and practical considerations for implementation.

1. The evidence for prevention

Multiple large prospective cohort studies have followed healthy adults over many years. A meta-analysis of 41 studies involving more than 266,000 participants found that individuals who engaged in physical activity were 37% less likely to develop depression than sedentary individuals.

The dose-response relationship is non-linear. Studies suggest that moderate to vigorous activity for 30 to 60 minutes, performed 3 to 5 times weekly, provides substantial protection. The protective effect appears to plateau at higher volumes, with no evidence of additional benefit from extreme exercise levels.

2. The evidence for treatment

2.1 Major depressive disorder

Meta-analytic evidence consistently shows that exercise reduces depressive symptoms, with effect sizes ranging from moderate to large (d = 0.50 to 0.80) compared to control conditions.

Comparison with standard treatments:
- Exercise alone shows comparable efficacy to established treatments like antidepressant medication and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) in mild to moderate depression.
- Combined approaches (exercise plus conventional treatment) yield superior outcomes compared to standard treatment alone, with effect sizes of approximately d = 0.60 to 0.80.
- Exercise also reduces the risk of relapse, with a meta-analysis showing that exercise alone or combined with standard treatment reduces recurrence risk by approximately 25%.

2.2 Depression severity

The therapeutic effect appears consistent across depression severity levels:
- Mild depression: exercise as a stand-alone intervention shows strong efficacy
- Moderate depression: exercise combined with conventional treatment shows the most robust outcomes
- Severe depression: exercise alone is less effective than pharmacological or psychotherapeutic interventions, though it can serve as an effective adjunct

3. Biological mechanisms

3.1 Neurotransmitters

Exercise affects several neurotransmitter systems implicated in depression:
- Serotonin: acute and chronic exercise increases serotonin synthesis, release and receptor density, particularly in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus
- Dopamine: increased dopamine release in the striatum and mesolimbic pathways contributes to exercise-induced mood elevation
- Norepinephrine: exercise increases its release and turnover
- Endocannabinoids: endogenous cannabinoids like anandamide increase after exercise and may contribute to the "runner's high"

3.2 Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF)

Exercise consistently elevates BDNF levels in both patients with depression and healthy controls. BDNF plays a crucial role in:
- Neurogenesis: the generation of new neurons, particularly in the hippocampus, which shows volume reduction in depressed individuals
- Synaptic plasticity: the brain's ability to form new connections and adapt
- Neuroprotection: the survival of existing neurons

3.3 Hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis regulation

Chronic stress activates the HPA axis, leading to elevated cortisol levels, which are associated with depression. Exercise:
- Normalizes HPA axis function
- Reduces cortisol reactivity to psychological stress
- Increases glucocorticoid receptor sensitivity

3.4 Inflammatory markers

Elevated inflammatory markers like C-reactive protein, interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) are associated with depression. Exercise:
- Reduces systemic inflammation
- Increases anti-inflammatory cytokines like IL-10
- May attenuate the inflammatory response induced by stress

3.5 Neuroendocrine changes

Exercise affects several neuroendocrine factors:
- Opioid peptides: endorphins and enkephalins, which contribute to exercise-induced euphoria
- Oxytocin: increased after exercise, with potential social and stress-buffering effects

3.6 Other mechanisms
- Increased cerebral blood flow and angiogenesis
- Enhanced mitochondrial function
- Improved sleep quality
- Increased self-efficacy and sense of accomplishment

4. Optimal exercise parameters

4.1 Type

Multiple exercise modalities show antidepressant effects:
- Aerobic exercise: running, walking, cycling, swimming
- Resistance training: weight lifting, bodyweight exercises
- Mind-body practices: yoga, tai chi, qigong
- Combination approaches that include both aerobic and resistance components

Comparative studies do not consistently identify one modality as superior. Individual preference and practical considerations appear more important than modality-specific effects.

4.2 Frequency

The antidepressant effect of exercise follows an inverted U-shaped dose-response relationship:
- Moderate frequency (3 to 5 days per week) shows optimal effects
- Frequency below 3 days per week shows diminished effects
- Frequency above 5 days per week may not provide additional benefit and may increase risk of injury and burnout

4.3 Duration

Effective exercise duration ranges from 45 to 60 minutes per session, though shorter bouts (20 to 30 minutes) still produce measurable antidepressant effects, particularly for individuals with sedentary lifestyles.

4.4 Intensity

Exercise intensity is measured using:
- Heart rate: moderate intensity corresponds to 50 to 70% of maximum heart rate
- Perceived exertion: ratings of 11 to 13 on the 6 to 20 Borg scale
- VO2 max: moderate intensity corresponds to 40 to 60% of VO2 max

Moderate intensity appears optimal for most individuals with depression, though higher intensities may be more effective for some, particularly younger individuals and those with mild to moderate depression.

4.5 Duration of intervention

Significant antidepressant effects are typically observed after 4 to 6 weeks of regular exercise, with continued improvements after 12 to 16 weeks. Maintenance of therapeutic effects requires continued exercise, as discontinuation typically results in gradual loss of benefits.

5. Special populations

5.1 Elderly individuals

Exercise is particularly effective in elderly populations:
- Reduces depression symptoms in older adults, including those with comorbid physical conditions
- Improves cognitive function
- Increases functional independence

5.2 Adolescents

Exercise shows effectiveness in adolescents with depression:
- Effective as a stand-alone intervention
- May be particularly effective for adolescents with mild to moderate depression
- Can reduce the risk of depression onset in at-risk adolescents

5.3 Perinatal women

Exercise during pregnancy and postpartum:
- Reduces depressive symptoms in pregnant women
- Shows promise as a preventive intervention for postpartum depression
- Is generally safe during pregnancy when performed at moderate intensity

5.4 Individuals with treatment-resistant depression

Exercise as an adjunctive intervention:
- Can be effective for individuals who do not respond to conventional treatments
- May help mitigate side effects of antidepressant medication
- May reduce the required dosage of medication

6. Barriers and challenges

6.1 Individual barriers
- Low motivation and energy, which are themselves symptoms of depression
- Lack of knowledge about exercise benefits
- Negative past experiences with exercise
- Body image concerns
- Physical limitations and comorbid health conditions
- Lack of time

6.2 Structural and environmental barriers
- Lack of access to exercise facilities
- Safety concerns in the surrounding environment
- Financial constraints
- Lack of social support

6.3 Clinical barriers
- Limited referral systems between mental health and physical health providers
- Lack of exercise prescription training among mental health professionals
- Limited integration of exercise into treatment guidelines
- Lack of systematic monitoring and follow-up

7. Recommendations

7.1 Clinical practice
- Systematic assessment of physical activity levels during routine psychiatric evaluations
- Development of individualized exercise prescription as part of comprehensive treatment plans
- Collaboration with exercise professionals, including physical therapists and certified exercise specialists

7.2 Public health
- Community-based exercise programs specifically designed for individuals with depression
- Increased access to exercise facilities in mental health treatment centers
- Public health campaigns promoting the mental health benefits of physical activity
- Integration of exercise promotion in primary care settings

7.3 Research
- Further randomized controlled trials comparing different exercise modalities, dosages and intensities
- Research on optimal exercise prescription for specific populations
- Investigation of long-term maintenance strategies
- Development and validation of measures to assess exercise adherence

8. Limitations of the current evidence

8.1 Methodological limitations
- Heterogeneity in exercise interventions across studies
- Small sample sizes in many studies
- Lack of standardized exercise prescription
- Short follow-up periods
- Inconsistent use of control conditions

8.2 Measurement limitations
- Reliance on self-report measures of physical activity
- Limited objective measures of exercise adherence
- Inconsistent assessment of depression severity and symptoms

8.3 Generalizability
- Limited representation of specific populations
- Underrepresentation of individuals with severe depression
- Limited studies in diverse cultural contexts

9. Conclusions

The evidence consistently demonstrates that regular physical activity is effective in preventing and treating depression, with moderate to vigorous intensity exercise for 30 to 60 minutes, 3 to 5 times weekly, showing optimal effects. The antidepressant effects of exercise are associated with multiple biological mechanisms, including neurotransmitter regulation, BDNF elevation, HPA axis normalization, and reduced inflammation. Exercise can serve as a stand-alone intervention for mild to moderate depression and as an effective adjunctive treatment for more severe cases. Despite the evidence, exercise is not routinely prescribed or monitored in mental health care. Overcoming barriers to implementation requires coordinated efforts among clinicians, public health professionals, and researchers. Further research is needed to determine optimal exercise parameters for specific populations and to develop effective long-term maintenance strategies.

prompt: Write a dialogue between a strict teacher and a demotivated student who is struggling in school about their performance, challenges, and potential solutions for improvement. Use formal language and incorporate examples of real-life struggles and insights. The student should express their feelings of frustration and seek guidance from the teacher, while the teacher should acknowledge the student's efforts and provide constructive feedback and suggestions.

The bell had just rung. The corridor emptied, but Priya Sharma did not move from her desk.

"You have stayed behind for three days running, Sharma," said Mr. Keshav Nair. He did not look up from the ledger he was balancing. "If you are here for the extra problems, the answers are on the board. You may copy them and go."

"I did the problems. I got six of them wrong."

"Then you have done the work. The marks are a separate matter."

"Is it that I am not clever enough? I have been wondering that for a year."

Nair closed the ledger. He was a tall man who carried his height as though it were an obligation. He walked to the window and looked out at the playground. "I have taught this class for eleven years. I can tell you what I have seen, though you should know how much I weigh what I say."

"Please."

"You are not slow at the work. I have watched you solve algebra in your head when the others are still writing down the formula. If you were dull, you would be failing arithmetic, and you are not." He turned back to her. "You are failing because you stop when it gets difficult, and you have been doing that for a year."

"That is not fair."

"Is it not? Show me the page where you stop."

She reached into her bag and pulled out a crumpled worksheet. He scanned it and pointed to the third question.

"Here. You knew the method. The numbers got large, the fraction was messy, and you went back to the question at the top."

"That's a small thing."

"A small thing done every week adds up. But you can stop that. Here is what is not up to you. The board, the textbook, the teacher. And the mark. The mark is not up to you. What is up to you is how long you keep working on a problem when it gets ugly. I can tell you that because I have watched it happen in others."

He went back to his desk and pulled a fresh sheet of paper toward him. "Here is a problem. It is going to take you twenty minutes."

Priya picked up her pencil. "Can I ask you something? You seem to know a lot about this."

"I have taught for eleven years, and I have failed a great many students. I have also seen students who were exactly where you are now, and some of them are doing well. I want you to know this. I am not a psychologist. If things get worse, if you find you cannot sleep, or you begin to dread coming to school, go to the counsellor. That is no shame. It is what a smart girl does when she needs help."

Priya felt her face grow hot. "You think that is what is happening."

"I think you are tired and frustrated. I would like to see you in a month. Can you come back at the same time next week?"

She hesitated, then nodded.

"Good. Now, the problem."

The classroom fell silent around them, the way a room does when someone is working hard at something. Priya did not speak again until she reached the second step.

"Is this right?"

Nair looked at her working for a long moment. "The method is correct. The arithmetic is not quite there. Go back and check."

She checked. She found her mistake, corrected it, and looked up with a small smile.

"Good. That is a real correction, Sharma. A correctable error is the best news you could have had this week."

She picked up her bag. "Thank you."

"Wait." He handed her the worksheet. "Take this home. Do all of it, every question. If you get stuck, do not stop. Mark it and come back to it tomorrow."

She looked at him, surprised. "You would give me homework?"

"I am giving you a problem that will take twenty minutes. The rest is yours."

She left, walking a little faster than she had come.

## Slide 1: Title
**Stolen Beauty: The Case for Using Up Materials in Art and Craft**
[Your name]

## Slide 2: The problem
On a typical day, a maker uses a little of a material and throws away the rest. The leftover goes into a drawer. A few years later the drawer is full, and the material is dry, damaged, or out of fashion. The maker buys new, and the cycle continues.

This happens whether the material is expensive or cheap. It happens with fabric, wood, paper, paint, and even digital assets.

[Visual: a page from Beuys's scrapbook]

## Slide 6: The case for using up materials
Using up materials is a way of honoring them. When you use every part of a material, you are showing that you value it and that you don't take it for granted.

[Visual: a close-up of a hand holding a small piece of fabric, with a large piece in the background]

---

## Slide 7: The case for using up materials, continued
Using up materials is also a way of reducing waste. When you use every part of a material, you don't need to buy as much and you don't create as much waste.

[Visual: a diagram showing the amount of waste created by a maker who uses up materials compared to one who doesn't]

---

## Slide 8: The case for using up materials, continued
Using up materials is also a way of expressing yourself. When you use scraps, you are forced to think creatively and to come up with new and innovative ideas.

---

## Slide 9: Interactive demonstration
[Activity: "What would you make with this?"]
Show your audience a variety of scraps and have them work in small groups to come up with ideas for what they could create with them. Encourage them to think beyond the obvious and to use their imagination.

### Notes for the presenter

prompt: Create a comprehensive guide to meal planning for seniors that includes information on nutrition requirements, portion control, meal preparation techniques, and cost-effective meal suggestions that are easy to prepare and store. The guide should be presented in an easy-to-read format with simple language, and should also address any common health issues that seniors face such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and heart disease. Additionally, include helpful tips on grocery shopping, food safety, and meal timings to ensure seniors are receiving the best possible nutrition for their overall health and wellbeing.
completion:
Eating well after sixty-five is mostly about small changes. Your body needs less fuel, but it still needs all the vitamins, minerals, protein and water it did when you were thirty. This guide will help you plan meals that are healthy, cheap and not too much trouble.

1. What you need

Energy: Most older people need fewer calories than they did. A sedentary woman may need around 1,600 to 1,800 a day and a man 1,800 to 2,000. If you are still cooking and clearing up after yourself, you will need more. Ask your doctor for a number for you.

Protein: Crucial if you are to keep your muscle, and muscle is what lets you get up from a chair and climb stairs. Aim for 25 to 30 grams at each meal. Sources: eggs, fish, chicken, pork, tofu, beans, lentils, Greek yoghurt, cottage cheese, milk, cheese, nuts.

Fibre: Helps digestion and helps control blood sugar and cholesterol. Aim for twenty-five grams a day from fruit, vegetables, whole grains and legumes.

Calcium and Vitamin D: Needed for bone health. Sources of calcium: milk, yoghurt, cheese, fortified plant milks, sardines, tofu, dark leafy greens. Vitamin D is hard to get from food. Most people need it as a supplement, especially in winter. Ask your doctor to check your levels.

Water: The thirst signal fades with age, and you may not feel thirsty even when you need a drink. Aim for about eight cups of fluid a day. Water, tea, coffee, milk, soup all count.

2. Portion control

Your stomach shrinks with age, so smaller plates help. An 8 to 10 inch plate can make a small portion look generous. A large plate makes you fill it, and then you eat too much.

A simple plate model for lunch and dinner: half your plate non-starchy vegetables, a quarter protein, a quarter complex carbohydrate.

Common mistakes: drinking your calories (soda, juice, milkshakes), grazing on biscuits and crackers throughout the day, and eating the family portion because you are ashamed to ask for less. All of these add up to more than you realise.

3. Simple techniques for meal preparation

Cook in bulk: When you feel up to it, make large batches of soups, stews, curries, casseroles and pasta bakes. Portion them into containers and freeze them.

Double the recipe: When you cook a meal you enjoy, make enough for tomorrow.

Chop in advance: Wash and chop vegetables after shopping and store them in sealed containers. They will be ready to use when tired.

Use the microwave and slow cooker: These let you prepare a meal with very little effort.

Soften the texture: If you have trouble chewing, use ingredients like avocado, mashed potatoes, slow cooked meats, soups and stews.

4. Cost-effective meal suggestions

Breakfast: Oatmeal made with milk or water, topped with fruit and a handful of nuts; scrambled eggs on whole grain toast; Greek yoghurt with berries; a smoothie with spinach, frozen banana and milk.

Lunch: Tuna or chicken salad on whole grain bread; vegetable soup with a slice of cheese and a side salad; a leftover dinner portion.

Dinner: Baked or grilled chicken with vegetables; fish with rice; lentil stew; pasta primavera with grilled tofu.

Snacks: Fresh or dried fruit; a piece of cheese; a handful of unsalted almonds; a boiled egg; carrot sticks with hummus.

5. Health conditions

Diabetes: Keep to regular meal times so that your blood sugar doesn't drop too low between meals. Keep your carbohydrate portions consistent. Choose whole grains, fruit, vegetables and legumes. Reduce processed foods and sugary drinks.

High blood pressure: Limit salt, as it raises blood pressure. Avoid canned soups, processed meats, pickles and salty snacks. Use herbs, spices, garlic and lemon for flavour.

Heart disease: Reduce saturated fat by eating less red meat, butter and full-fat dairy. Increase your intake of omega-3 fatty acids, which are found in oily fish like salmon, mackerel and sardines.

Always consult with your doctor or a dietitian before making significant changes to your diet, especially if you have an existing health condition.

6. Grocery shopping

Make a list and stick to it: This will help you avoid impulse purchases.

Shop the perimeter: Shop the outer edges of the store, where fresh produce, dairy, meat and fish are usually found.

Buy in bulk: Larger packages are often cheaper per unit. Check the price per 100g or 1kg to compare. Buy frozen or canned fruit and vegetables, which are often cheaper than fresh and just as nutritious.

Don't shop hungry: You are more likely to make unhealthy choices when you are hungry.

7. Food safety

Cook meat, poultry and fish thoroughly: Use a food thermometer to ensure that it has reached the recommended internal temperature to kill harmful bacteria.

Reheat leftovers thoroughly: If you are reheating leftovers, ensure that they are steaming hot throughout.

Store food properly: Raw meat should be stored on the bottom shelf of the fridge to prevent it from dripping onto other foods.

Clean surfaces regularly: Wash your hands, countertops and utensils after handling raw meat, poultry or fish.

Check expiration dates: Don't eat food past its use-by date.

Follow the "2-hour rule": Perishable food should not be left out at room temperature for more than two hours.

8. Meal timings

Eat regular meals: Try to eat breakfast, lunch and dinner at regular times each day. This will help your body to get into a rhythm and prevent you from overeating later in the day.

Limit snacks: Snacking between meals can add up to a lot of calories and can also reduce your appetite for正餐 (main meals).

Have a light evening meal: Eating a large meal late at night can cause indigestion and affect your sleep.

If you live alone, consider meal delivery services, community meals, or cooking with a friend or family member.

completion:
The program's logic is sound, but the documentation, indentation and variable naming need substantial attention. Let me work through what the program does. It builds a graph of the board's cells, where each cell is a node and adjacent cells are connected. It uses breadth-first search to find the shortest path from the starting position to the goal. The path length is measured in steps along the edges, meaning that moving diagonally between adjacent cells costs no extra distance.

Now let me go through the quality requirements one at a time.

The documentation is thin. It has a docstring for the main function, but nothing at all for the helper functions: `get_adjacent_cells`, `is_valid_move`, `find_shortest_path`, `get_manhattan_distance` and `print_board`. Each of these should have a docstring explaining what it does and its parameters. The code also lacks explanatory comments, so a reader would struggle to understand how the algorithm works.

The indentation is inconsistent. The `if __name__ == "__main__":` block is not indented. Function bodies should be indented by four spaces, and nested blocks like the `while` loop and the `for` loops inside it should be indented further.

Variable names are a mixed bag. `start`, `goal` and `board` are clear. `adjacent_cells` is a bit long but accurate. `neighbors` is a good choice. `visited` is adequate. But `path` is overloaded, serving as both the current path and the shortest path. `q` for the queue is a standard convention, though `queue` would be clearer.

One more consideration: the program should handle edge cases gracefully. For example, if the starting cell is the same as the goal cell, the program should handle it without error.

Here is the corrected version:

```python
from collections import deque


def get_adjacent_cells(row, col, rows, cols):
    """Return list of adjacent cells (up, down, left, right)."""
    directions = [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]
    adjacent = []
    for dr, dc in directions:
        new_row, new_col = row + dr, col + dc
        if 0 <= new_row < rows and 0 <= new_col < cols:
            adjacent.append((new_row, new_col))
    return adjacent


def is_valid_move(start, end, board):
    """Return True if the move is valid (within bounds and not on an obstacle)."""
    row, col = start
    end_row, end_col = end
    if 0 <= end_row < len(board) and 0 <= end_col < len(board[0]):
        return board[end_row][end_col] != '#'
    return False


def find_shortest_path(start, goal, board):
    """Find shortest path from start to goal using BFS.
    
    Path length is measured in steps along edges, so moving diagonally
    between adjacent cells costs no extra distance.
    """
    rows, cols = len(board), len(board[0])
    queue = deque([(start, [start])])
    visited = set([start])
    
    while queue:
        current, path = queue.popleft()
        
        if current == goal:
            return path
        
        for neighbor in get_adjacent_cells(current[0], current[1], rows, cols):
            if neighbor not in visited and is_valid_move(current, neighbor, board):
                visited.add(neighbor)
                queue.append((neighbor, path + [neighbor]))
    
    return None


def get_manhattan_distance(start, goal):
    """Calculate Manhattan distance between two points."""
    row_diff = abs(start[0] - goal[0])
    col_diff = abs(start[1] - goal[1])
    return row_diff + col_diff


def print_board(board, path=None):
    """Print the board with the path highlighted (if provided)."""
    for row_idx, row in enumerate(board):
        for col_idx, cell in enumerate(row):
            if path and (row_idx, col_idx) in path:
                print('P', end='')
            else:
                print(cell, end='')
        print()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Define the maze
    maze = [
        ['S', '.', '.', '.', '.'],
        ['#', '#', '.', '#', '.'],
        ['.', '.', '.', '.', '.'],
        ['.', '#', '#', '#', '.'],
        ['.', '.', '.', '.', 'E'],
    ]
    
    start_position = (0, 0)
    goal_position = (4, 4)
    
    print("Maze:")
    print_board(maze)
    print()
    
    shortest_path = find_shortest_path(start_position, goal_position, maze)
    
    if shortest_path:
        print(f"Shortest path found: {shortest_path}")
        print(f"Path length: {len(shortest_path) - 1} steps")
        print(f"Manhattan distance: {get_manhattan_distance(start_position, goal_position)}")
        print()
        print("Path on the map:")
        print_board(maze, shortest_path)
    else:
        print("No path found from start to goal.")
```

The corrections are straightforward. The `if __name__ == "__main__":` block is now indented. Every function has a docstring. `q` has been replaced with `queue` and `path` with `current` to distinguish the two uses. The `print_board` function now accepts an optional `path` parameter to highlight the solution.

prompt: Write a research paper evaluating the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using blockchain for property transactions and management. Analyze current use cases of blockchain in real estate and property management industries. Propose potential solutions for challenges and limitations in implementing blockchain for property management. Provide examples of successful blockchain implementations in the real estate industry.

For the journal of property management studies, volume 12, issue 3 (hypothetical)

The promise of blockchain in property management

Abstract

Property management relies on records that all parties trust: titles, leases, payment histories and maintenance logs. This paper asks whether distributed ledger technology can make those records more secure and less costly to verify. We find that the strengths of blockchain are most evident where a single party must convince many others of a fact, which is exactly where legacy systems are slowest. The weaknesses of the technology, however, are most acute in property management. The immutability that protects the record also preserves its errors, and a ledger cannot easily undo a mistaken entry. We propose a hybrid model in which the blockchain serves as a verification layer for records that remain in conventional databases. We find this in the case of the Swedish land registry, which has used blockchain to verify land transactions since 2016, reducing transaction times from weeks to days.

1. Introduction

The management of residential, commercial and industrial property involves many parties with competing interests: landlords, tenants, buyers, sellers, lenders, insurers, government regulators and property managers. The efficiency of this system depends on records that all parties can trust. Historically, trust has been maintained through centralized authorities such as county record offices, title insurance companies and notaries public, who maintain records that can be audited by law.

Blockchain technology promises to replace these centralized authorities with a distributed, cryptographically secure record that cannot be altered. When applied to property management, this could significantly reduce the costs of fraud prevention, streamline transactions, and provide transparent and immutable records of property history. This paper evaluates the potential of blockchain technology for secure property management, analyzing its advantages and disadvantages, current use cases, and proposing solutions to implementation challenges.

2. Theoretical framework

2.1 Core properties

Blockchain possesses several properties that are relevant to property management. First, it is decentralized, with no single point of failure and no central authority controlling the records. Second, it is cryptographically secure, using hashing and digital signatures to ensure that records cannot be altered without detection. Third, it is transparent and auditable, with all transactions visible to authorized participants. Fourth, it provides an immutable record, meaning that once a transaction is recorded, it cannot be deleted or altered.

2.2 Smart contracts

Smart contracts are self-executing contracts with the terms of the agreement directly written into code. They automatically enforce and execute the terms when predefined conditions are met. In property management, smart contracts could automate rent collection, lease renewals, maintenance requests and dispute resolution.

3. Advantages of blockchain for property management

3.1 Enhanced security

The most significant advantage of blockchain is its security. The cryptographic nature of the technology makes it nearly impossible to alter recorded information without detection. This is particularly important for property records, which have historically been vulnerable to fraud such as title fraud, forged documents and duplicate sales.

3.2 Reduced fraud

Blockchain can significantly reduce fraud in property transactions. A distributed ledger means that there is no single record that can be altered by a dishonest party, and every transaction is verified by multiple nodes in the network. For example, a blockchain-based property registry could prevent title fraud by maintaining a permanent record of ownership that cannot be falsified.

3.3 Transparency and auditability

All transactions on a blockchain are visible to authorized participants, providing a transparent and auditable record of property history. This is particularly useful for property managers who must provide accurate records for accounting, tax purposes and regulatory compliance.

3.4 Faster transactions

Blockchain can significantly speed up property transactions by eliminating intermediaries such as title insurance companies, escrow agents and attorneys. The Swedish land registry's blockchain-based system has been shown to reduce property transaction times from weeks to days.

3.5 Lower costs

By reducing the need for intermediaries and manual verification processes, blockchain can significantly lower the costs of property transactions and management.

4. Current use cases in real estate and property management

4.1 Property title management

Several governments have begun implementing blockchain for property title management. Sweden's Lantmäteriet has been using blockchain to verify land transactions since 2016. The United Arab Emirates has launched the "Dubai Blockchain Strategy" to put all government transactions on blockchain by 2020. China has begun implementing blockchain for real estate registration in several cities.

4.2 Property management platforms

Several companies have developed blockchain-based property management platforms that streamline lease management, rent collection and tenant screening. Examples include Propy, which facilitates real estate transactions on blockchain, and RentChain, which uses blockchain for rental agreements and payment processing.

4.3 Property tokenization

Tokenization involves dividing property ownership into digital tokens that can be bought and sold on a blockchain. This allows fractional ownership of real estate, making property investment more accessible to smaller investors. Companies like RealT and Rebal have pioneered this approach.

4.4 Smart contracts for leasing

Smart contracts are being used to automate lease agreements, including rent collection, security deposits and lease renewals. The Ethereum blockchain platform supports various blockchain applications for lease management.

5. Disadvantages and limitations

5.1 Immutability

The immutability of blockchain is both its greatest strength and its most significant limitation. Once a record is added to the blockchain, it cannot be erased or corrected. This means that mistakes in property records, such as incorrect boundary descriptions or erroneous ownership information, cannot be easily rectified. In traditional systems, errors can be corrected through legal processes and official amendments.

5.2 Scalability

Current blockchain networks face scalability challenges, with many unable to handle the volume of transactions that real estate systems require. For example, the Bitcoin network can process only a limited number of transactions per second.

5.3 Legal and regulatory challenges

The legal status of blockchain-based property records is unclear in many jurisdictions. Laws and regulations governing real estate transactions were written with centralized systems in mind and may not accommodate distributed ledgers. The recognition of smart contracts as legally binding contracts is still being established in many legal systems.

5.4 Interoperability

5.5 Cost

5.6 Energy consumption

6. Proposed solutions

6.1 Hybrid implementation

We propose a hybrid model in which the blockchain serves as a verification layer for records that remain in conventional databases. In this model, property records are maintained in traditional systems, and blockchain is used to verify and timestamp critical transactions and changes. This allows for corrections to be made to the records when necessary, while still providing the security and auditability benefits of blockchain.

6.2 Off-chain storage

To address scalability and cost concerns, property records can be stored off-chain in conventional databases, with only critical information hashed and stored on the blockchain. This reduces the load on the blockchain while maintaining the security of important data.

6.3 Layer 2 scaling solutions

Layer 2 solutions, such as payment channels and sidechains, can increase the transaction capacity of blockchain networks. These solutions process transactions off the main blockchain and only record the final results, significantly increasing throughput.

6.4 Consensus mechanism optimization

Transitioning from Proof of Work to more efficient consensus mechanisms, such as Proof of Stake, can reduce energy consumption and increase transaction speeds. The Ethereum blockchain's planned transition to Proof of Stake is an example of this approach.

6.5 Regulatory frameworks

Stakeholders should work with legislators to develop regulatory frameworks that recognize blockchain-based property records and smart contracts. Early engagement with regulatory bodies can help shape these frameworks.

6.6 Standardization

Industry-wide standards for blockchain data formats and interfaces can improve interoperability between different blockchain systems. Organizations like the Real Estate Standards Organization (RESO) can play a key role in developing these standards.

7. Case studies

7.1 Sweden

Sweden's Lantmäteriet (National Land Survey) has been using blockchain technology to verify land transactions since 2016. 8. Future directions

The future of blockchain in property management will depend on several factors, including technological advancements, regulatory developments and industry adoption. We expect to see increased adoption of hybrid implementation models, improved interoperability between systems, and more sophisticated smart contracts for automated property management.

9. Conclusion

Blockchain technology offers significant potential for enhancing security and efficiency in property management. Its cryptographic security, transparency and immutability make it well-suited for managing property records and transactions. However, its limitations, particularly its immutability and scalability issues, require careful consideration in implementation. We propose a hybrid model that addresses these limitations while retaining the security benefits of blockchain. Success will require collaboration between industry stakeholders, technologists and regulators to develop standards and frameworks that support blockchain adoption in property management.
